extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and media history; journalists studying press ethics and news production
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and evaluative standards for newspaper practice (late-19th/early-20th century U.S. press), especially the techniques and ethics of 'yellow journalism'. Useful for assessing news content, layout, and production choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism (crime, scandal, disasters, sports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow journalism was founded upon the familiar aspects of sensationalism— crime news, scandal and gossip, divorces and sex, and stress upon the reporting of disasters and sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics function as circulation pullers. The text treats them as core content elements of sensational papers; acceptable in moderation but when emphasized to the exclusion of accuracy they become part of 'yellow' practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scare-heads / banner heads (excessively large type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scare-heads, in which excessively large type, printed in either black or red, screamed excitement, often about comparatively unimportant news, thus giving a shrill falsity to the entire make-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of very large, blackened, or red banner headlines was a distinguishing technique; they grab attention but can misrepresent importance. Examples: full-width banner lines, hand-drawn block type several inches high, red streamer heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lavish use of pictures (and picture abuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lavish use of pictures, many of them without significance, inviting the abuses of picture-stealing and 'faked' pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy pictorial content and illustrated features can enhance appeal, but the page warns of picture-stealing and fabrication as common abuses—an anti-pattern for ethical reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impostures and frauds (faked interviews/stories, misleading heads, pseudo-science)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impostures and frauds of various kinds, such as 'faked' interviews and stories, misleading heads, pseudo-science, and parade of false learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constitute dishonest practices: inventing interviews, publishing pseudo-scientific claims, and deceptive headlines. Examples in text include planted fake casualty names and contrived dispatches; score negatively for integrity and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunday supplement (colored comics and superficial articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sunday supplement, with colored comics and superficial articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunday supplements introduced entertainment-focused content (comics, lightweight features). Seen as part of yellow technique—appealing to broad readership but criticized for superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ostentatious sympathy with the 'underdog' / campaign journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: More or less ostentatious sympathy with the 'underdog,' with campaigns against abuses suffered by the common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing coverage as advocacy for the underdog can be legitimate, but when used ostentatiously as a circulation tactic it becomes a hallmark of yellow practice; evaluate sincerity and evidence behind campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and avoidance of gross misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Gross misrepresentation of the facts, deliberate invention of tales calculated to excite the public, and wanton recklessness in the construction of headlines’ (Godkin’s condemnation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core ethical metric: do not invent facts or distort events to excite readers. The text treats such behavior as 'disgraceful' and grounds for severe criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: False eyewitness and attribution claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubtless many of the incidents reported were not witnessed by the correspondents, and too much reliance was placed on the exaggerated tales of the Cubans; there were cases ... of correspondents who wrote 'eye-witness' stories when they had approached no nearer to the scene than Key West.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming eyewitness status when not present is an ethical violation. Verify presence, sourcing, and labeling of reports; label such claims an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing/staging news and propaganda (making as well as recording news)
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalism which makes as well as records news must— occasionally, at least— do a brilliant bit in the actual fighting. (Examples: staged rescue of Evangelina Cisneros, Hearst’s reported attitude 'you furnish the pictures and I'll furnish the war').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish reporting from manufacturing events for publicity or propaganda. Staging, orchestrating rescues, or deliberately inciting public sentiment counts against impartial reporting and can amount to war-mongering or propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical proprietorial intervention and direct participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearst personally led a force of writers, artists, and photographers; furnished a small printing plant on his flagship; staged receptions and delivered prisoners—blurring the line between proprietor and correspondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners or editors actively participating in events or publicity stunts complicate editorial independence. Evaluate conflicts of interest and the degree to which proprietorial theatrics shape coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline design revolution (permanent effects and excesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The enlargement and blackening of headlines, introduction of the single-line full-width front-page banner, outline and Gothic types, and streamer lines—practices that revolutionized front-page makeup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize headline design as both a legitimate innovation (clear, prominent banners) and a potential excess (monstrous confusion, lawless front-page make-up). Assess proportionality and relation of headline to story importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic incentives and production costs vs. profitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuban atrocity stories proved to be good circulation pullers... Few newspapers increased profits during the Spanish-American War ... competition in extras was expensive ... cost of war coverage was immense (chartering ships, many correspondents, cable tolls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news decisions against economic realities: high-cost coverage and aggressive extra editions can boost circulation but may not be profitable; consider sustainability and whether editorial choices are driven by revenue-seeking rather than public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / news-lifting and rivalry tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes of news theft and reciprocal tricks (e.g., planting fake names to detect lifting: 'Reflipe W. Thenuz' and 'Lister A. Raah').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality and proper sourcing are metrics of journalistic quality. The text documents competitive tactics and counter-tactics; copying rivals' dispatches without attribution is condemned and flagged as unethical practice.
